name: Database Replication
intent: Keep copies of the same data on several database servers, to serve more reads and to survive the loss of a machine.
scenario: A shop's database receives a few writes and a huge number of reads. One server is overloaded by the reads, and if it fails the shop is offline.
problem: A single database is a bottleneck for reads and a single point of failure. A faster machine only postpones the problem, and if the server or its disk dies, the data and the service go with it.

howItWorks.title: Writes go to one primary
howItWorks.text: In the common leader-follower setup, all writes are applied by a single primary (leader). That keeps a single, ordered history of changes and avoids conflicting writes.

howItWorks.title: Changes stream to replicas
howItWorks.text: The primary records every change in a log and ships it to replicas (followers), which apply the same changes in the same order. Each replica ends up as a copy of the primary.

howItWorks.title: Reads can be served by replicas
howItWorks.text: Read traffic is spread across the replicas, multiplying read capacity. The write path is unchanged, so replication helps read-heavy workloads the most.

howItWorks.title: Replication lag causes stale reads
howItWorks.text: With asynchronous replication the primary acknowledges a write immediately, and replicas catch up moments later. A read from a replica in that window returns old data, so a user may not see their own change. Synchronous replication waits for replicas to confirm, which removes the gap but makes every write slower.

howItWorks.title: Failover promotes a replica
howItWorks.text: If the primary dies, the most up-to-date replica is promoted to be the new primary. With asynchronous replication, writes the old primary acknowledged but had not yet sent are lost. Two nodes both believing they are primary (split brain) is a serious risk that failover systems must prevent.

pros: Read capacity grows with the number of replicas
Survives machine failure: another copy can take over
Replicas can be placed near users, or used for backups and analytics
Maintenance and upgrades can be done one node at a time
cons: Replicas can serve stale data (replication lag)
Does not increase write capacity or the amount of data you can store
Failover can lose recent writes, or cause split brain if done badly
More servers to operate, monitor and keep in sync
whenToUse: Read-heavy workloads: product catalogs, profiles, feeds
You need high availability and a copy for disaster recovery
You need an isolated copy for reporting that does not slow production
whenNotToUse: The load is write-heavy or the data is too large for one machine: that needs sharding
Every read must see the latest write and the cost of waiting is unacceptable
A single well-backed-up database is enough for your traffic and uptime needs
pitfalls: Reading your own write from a lagging replica, so the user's change seems to vanish
Assuming a replica is a backup: a bad delete or corrupt write is replicated too
Automatic failover without safeguards, creating two primaries
Ignoring lag until it grows to minutes under heavy load

roles.label: Primary
roles.description: Accepts writes and ships the change log.

roles.label: Replica
roles.description: A copy that applies the log and serves reads.

quiz.question: A shop runs one primary and two asynchronous replicas. The primary's disk fails right after it acknowledged an order. The most up-to-date replica is about 2 seconds behind and is promoted. What is the likely outcome?
options: Nothing is lost, because replicas hold an exact copy at all times even if the primary dies suddenly.
Orders acknowledged in the last couple of seconds may be missing on the new primary.
The replica refuses promotion until it has fully caught up with the dead primary's log.
The lost orders are replayed from the other replica's own log.
quiz.explanation: Asynchronous replication acknowledges before the replicas have the change, so a failover can drop recent writes. The only complete record of them was on the failed primary. Synchronous replication would close the gap at the cost of slower writes.

quiz.question: An order-ingest primary runs at 90 percent CPU, almost all of it from inserts. The team plans to add three more read replicas to relieve it. What do you expect?
options: Good relief, because the replicas will take a fair share of the insert work from the primary during heavy write periods.
Good relief, because replicas apply the same changes faster than the primary itself can.
Good relief, as long as the replicas are made synchronous so they share the write load.
Little relief, because every write still lands on the single primary.
quiz.explanation: Replicas copy the primary's changes; they do not accept writes in a leader-follower setup. They multiply read capacity only. Write-bound load needs a bigger primary, batching or sharding.

quiz.question: At 14:00 an engineer runs a bad DELETE that removes a million rows. The team notices at 14:20 and says 'we have three replicas, so we can recover from one'. What is the problem with this plan?
options: The delete replicated within seconds, so the replicas lost the rows too. Restore from a point-in-time backup.
The replicas keep a snapshot from the previous day, but it is days out of date.
A replica that is far behind must be promoted, and then it can serve the old rows.
Synchronous replicas would have refused the delete, so only asynchronous ones lose data and sync was needed.
quiz.explanation: A replica applies every change, including mistakes, so it is a copy and not a backup. After 20 minutes all replicas have applied the delete. Recovery needs a backup with point-in-time restore.
